review_comments.author: Yury Norov
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Yury Norov noted that N_MEMORY has two meanings today: whether a node has memory and whether ordinary allocations can use its memory, but once private nodes are introduced, these meanings diverge. He suggested keeping N_MEMORY meaning unchanged and adding another type, like N_MEMORY_NOALLOC.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 20, 2026 at 01:08:51PM -0500, Gregory Price via B4 Relay wrote:
> This is v6 of the Private NUMA node series. The series falls into four
> parts, each building on the one before:
> 
>    1-18  mm: introduce N_MEMORY_COMMON

I walked through this part, mostly. It looks like you can substantially
decrease the patch count if you keep N_MEMORY meaning unchanged, and
add another type, like N_MEMORY_NOALLOC.

>   19-26  restrict folio-walking MM services to common memory
>   27-44  N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, kept out of cpusets, mempolicy, accounting
>          and the page allocator's ordinary paths
>   45-61  private node features, memory hotplug of private memory,
>          dax/kmem private mode, selftests and documentation
> 
> Patches 1-26 change no behavior on any system and can be reviewed and
> merged on their own. Without private nodes, every path in patches 27-61
> behaves as before.
> 
> The full stack is also available at:
> https://github.com/gourryinverse/linux/tree/scratch/gourry/managed_nodes/private_nodes_v6
> 
> Motivation
> ==========
> 
> Some memory should be visible as a NUMA node without becoming part of
> the general allocation pool: HBM, coherent GPU or accelerator memory,
> or device memory a driver hands out itself.
> 
> Today such memory is either ordinary System RAM, where any allocation
> can fall back onto it and every MM service manages it, or ZONE_DEVICE,
> where the buddy allocator and the MM services are not available at all.
> 
> Private nodes sit in between. Their memory is managed by the buddy
> allocator, but ordinary allocations never land on it, and generic MM
> services leave it alone unless the node opts back in.
> 
> Model
> =====
> 
>   N_MEMORY = N_MEMORY_COMMON + N_MEMORY_PRIVATE
> 
>   - N_MEMORY keeps meaning "this node has memory".
>   - N_MEMORY_COMMON means ordinary allocations and kernel services
>     may use it.
>   - Allocation isolation comes from the zonelists: a private node is
>     on no fallback zonelist and has an empty __GFP_THISNODE zonelist.
>     It is reached only through its own private zonelist.
>   - Services that walk existing folios check folio_is_common_memory()
>     where they already skip ZONE_DEVICE.
>   - A private node can opt into compaction, reclaim and userspace
>     placement through per-node features. The services are written in
>     terms of their own node state (N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, ...), so services
>     don't need to be "aware" of anything but themselves.
> 
> The node state use / filtering model goes as such:
>   1) If you're walking the normal zonelists, you're already filtered
>   2) If you're walking nodelists to touch memory, filter on
>      N_MEMORY_COMMON by default (replacing N_MEMORY).
>   3) If you're walking structures to operate on folios / pages,
>      check folio_is_common_memory() (replacing zone_device checks)
>   4) If the service allows private memory interactions, use the
>      N_MEMORY_<FEATURE> bit corresponding to the service.
> 
>      e.g.: reclaim checks N_MEMORY_FEATURE when walking N_MEMORY
>      or when walking the private memory zonelist.
> 
> N_MEMORY_COMMON (patches 1-18)
> ==============================
> 
> N_MEMORY has two meanings today:
>   1) this node has memory
>   2) ordinary allocations and MM services can use this node's memory
> 
> The two are the same today. They stop being the same once a NUMA node
> with memory isn't part of the general allocation pool.
> 
> N_MEMORY_COMMON takes the second meaning, and the N_MEMORY users that
> mean it are converted. N_MEMORY continues reporting memory topology.
> 
> The rule for choosing between them:
> 
>   N_MEMORY         the node has memory: topology, per-node metadata and
>                    statistics, cpuset.mems.
>   N_MEMORY_COMMON  ordinary allocations or a kernel service may use the
>                    node's memory: zonelists, allocation and migration
>                    targets, per-node service threads, and sizing or
>                    accounting meant for ordinary allocations.
> 
> Code that walks the existing zonelist needs no check. The zonelists
> are built from N_MEMORY_COMMON, so they already hold only memory the
> allocation may use.
> 
> Unless a system actually has a private node, N_MEMORY and
> N_MEMORY_COMMON are the same set, so behavior should be unchanged.
> 
>   1-3   node-state helpers, N_MEMORY_COMMON itself, and the
>         `has_common_memory` sysfs ABI.
>   4     zonelists: the fallback lists hold common nodes, and a node's
>         __GFP_THISNODE list is built only for a common node
>   5-11  allocation and migration targets
>   12-13 kswapd and kcompactd
>   14-18 sizing and accounting meant for ordinary allocations
> 
> has_common_memory lists the same nodes as has_memory until memory
> outside N_MEMORY_COMMON exists. It is added now so that userspace, such
> as libnuma, can start choosing allocation targets from it, and so that
> the meaning is fixed before anything makes the two lists differ.
> 
> Folio-walking MM services (patches 19-26)
> =========================================
> 
> Patches 1-18 decide where memory comes from: zonelists, allocation
> targets and per-node services follow N_MEMORY_COMMON. Some MM services
> instead reach folios that already exist, wherever they are: through
> page tables (KSM, khugepaged, NUMA hinting, madvise, mbind() and
> migrate_pages(), move_pages()) or through physical addresses (DAMON).
> 
> These services skip ZONE_DEVICE folios with folio_is_zone_device() and
> page_is_zone_device().
> 
> Patch 19 generalizes those checks into folio_is_common_memory() and
> page_is_common_memory(), which reject ZONE_DEVICE folios and folios
> on a node outside N_MEMORY_COMMON.
> 
> The rule: a service that walks folios checks folio_is_common_memory()
> where it would otherwise check folio_is_zone_device().
> 
> Rather than add new hooks to page-table and pfn walkers, this reuses the
> places that already opt ZONE_DEVICE memory out.
> 
>   19    folio_is_common_memory() and page_is_common_memory()
>   20-26 ZONE_DEVICE checks in folio-walking services become
>         page/folio_is_common_memory(). One component per patch.
> 
> N_MEMORY_PRIVATE (patches 27-44)
> ================================
> 
> Patches 27-44 add the memory that makes N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_COMMON
> differ. A private node has online System RAM that ordinary allocations
> do not use and MM services leave alone, so neither an allocation that
> names no node nor a node-local kernel allocation can land on it.
> 
> Most of these patches add the explicit opt-outs that the N_MEMORY ->
> N_MEMORY_COMMON conversion did not cover, largely concentrated in
> cpuset, mempolicy and migration.
> 
> In the page allocator, each node gets a private zonelist holding its
> own zones only if it is private. MM code reaches private memory only
> through that zonelist (ALLOC_ZONELIST_PRIVATE plus a nodemask).
> 
> A private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes onto common
> memory, and exhausting private memory fails the allocation (SIGBUS on
> fault) instead of invoking the OOM killer (this can change in the
> future with additional work).
> 
> Nothing in patches 27-44 creates private memory. Memory hotplug of
> private memory, with dax/kmem as its first user, comes in patches
> 56-57, after the feature bits that let a private node opt into
> reclaim, compaction and userspace placement.
> 
>   27-28 N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, exported as has_private_memory.
>         A per-node feature mask on the pgdat.
>   29-30 accounting: MemTotal/MemFree/other limits ignore private mem.
>         the auto-movable online policy ignores private memory
>   31-35 cpusets and mempolicy: private nodes are inherited only on
>         request, never rebound onto, never spread over, and never
>         migrate_pages() destinations
>   36    explicit reclaim and compaction requests refuse private nodes
>   37-44 page allocator:
>         37-38 the reserves and watermarks, and contiguous allocation,
>               skip/refuse private memory
>         39-40 the private zonelist and its selection by MM callers
>         41    a private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes
>               onto common memory to ensure forward progress
>         42    exhausting private memory fails with SIGBUS, like an
>               exhausted HugeTLB pool
>         43    an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator (Brendan Jackman)
>         44    a bind policy whose nodes became private falls back to
>               common memory
> 
> Private node features and providers (patches 45-61)
> ===================================================
> 
> Patches 1-44 keep every generic MM service off private memory.
> 
> Some private memory wants a few of them back: HBM or coherent GPU
> memory that userspace manages with mbind() and migrate_pages() needs
> reclaim and compaction, while staying out of incidental allocation
> (no fallback onto it, only explicit placement).
> 
> Patches 45-55 add three opt-in feature bits and corresponding node
> states:
> 
>   N_MEMORY_COMPACTION   kcompactd, proactive and explicit compaction
>   N_MEMORY_RECLAIM      kswapd, memcg and explicit reclaim
>   N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY    mbind() and explicit migration may target it
> 
> The states cover what the kernel does on its own initiative. Direct
> reclaim and compaction serve an allocation within its own zonelist, so
> an allocation from a private node may reclaim and compact it either way.
> 
> RECLAIM requires COMPACTION, and MEMPOLICY requires both. Userspace
> control (mbind, migration) generates fragmentation, and as a result
> private allocations would fail unpredictably without reclaim/compaction.
> 
> Relcaim and compaction are required by mempolicy because otherwise
> order-N allocations cause unpredictable out of memory conditions due
> to fragmentation.
> 
> Demotion and NUMA balancing support are deferred to a later series
> but can be trivially support to allow demotions from HBM to DRAM
> as a way of cheap tiering.
> 
> Every common node carries all three, so the existing N_MEMORY_COMMON
> users that mean "reclaim" or "compaction" move to the new states.
> 
> Service support:
> 
>   45-46 N_MEMORY_COMPACTION, and compaction switched to it
>   47-48 N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, and reclaim switched to it
>   49    madvise reclaim advice only for reclaim-capable memory
>   50    memcg reclaim also visits private nodes that permit reclaim
>   51    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY
>   52    explicit migration acts on N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory
>   53    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory counts as general-purpose.
>         MemAvailable (free and file pages) and dirty limits count
> 	only common memory.
>   54    MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES: mbind() flag that binds a mapping to
>         one private node.
>   55    migrate_pages() support for N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY nodes
> 
> Creating a private node
> 
>   56    memory hotplug of private memory, with a feature mask
>   57    dax/kmem private mode
> 
> Testing and Documentation:
> 
>   58-60 selftests: private kmem devices and services, memory policy
>         bindings, migration and exhaustion, and cpuset interaction
>   61    Documentation/mm/numa_private_nodes.rst
> 
> MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES is new uapi. Without it, private nodes in an
> mbind() mask are ignored, similar to nodes outside the cpuset.
> 
> libnuma and numactl need a matching change to reach private nodes.
> 
> There is no sysfs list of the nodes that accept private bindings.
> userspace can probe with MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES.  Otherwise - we can
> discuss how service support should be discoverable to userspace.
> 
> Memory hotplug is the only source of private memory right now.
> 
> All System RAM on a node shares one configuration: hotplug with a
> different one fails with -EBUSY.
> 
> Costs and known limits
> ======================
> 
>   - ZONELIST_PRIVATE is a third zonelist per pgdat; with NODES_SHIFT=10
>     that is about 80KB per possible node, though a private zonelist
>     holds at most one node's zones.
> 
>     local-only zonelists can be space-optimized if this matters.
> 
>   - Free page reporting reports free private pages like any others.
> 
>   - Tasks are OOM-scored by all of their resident memory,
>     private pages included.
> 
> Changes since v5 ("Private Memory NUMA Nodes")
> ==============================================
> 
>   - Reordered so the N_MEMORY audit (patches 1-26) comes first and can
>     be reviewed (and merged) on its own if desired.
>   - Capabilities became memory features with node states, so a service
>     can be written in terms of itself: reclaim walks N_MEMORY_RECLAIM,
>     compaction N_MEMORY_COMPACTION.
>   - The capability set is pared down to COMPACTION, RECLAIM and
>     MEMPOLICY for the first run.  DEMOTION, NUMA_BALANCING, and
>     compressed RAM support are deferred.
>   - The private zonelist is now local-only. A fallback variant can be
>     added if a use case needs one.
>   - cpuset and OOM semantics are worked out:
>       - cpuset.mems governs private nodes
>       - private-only request inherits the parent's common nodes.
>   - Private bindings are an explicit uapi flag, MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES,
>     rather than inferred from the nodemask.
>   - Exhausting private placement fails the fault with SIGBUS, as an
>     exhausted HugeTLB pool does, instead of invoking the OOM killer.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/3] mm/page_alloc: drop the pcp lock before enabling IRQs after a drain
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation code by restoring IRQs only after dropping the per-cpu (pcp) lock, rather than enabling them while still holding the pcp lock. This prevents softirqs from failing to acquire the pcp lock and falling back to taking zone->lock, which can lead to contention and performance issues. The patch also includes a test case that demonstrates the improvement in throughput and callback duration on a 128-vCPU guest system.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/3] mm/page_alloc: drop the pcp lock before enabling IRQs after a refill
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation code by dropping the per-cpu page list (pcp) lock before enabling interrupts after refilling an empty pcp list. This is necessary because, when IRQs are disabled, an interrupt can occur while the pcp lock is held, causing softirqs to take the zone lock for each page. The patch improves performance in a 128-vCPU guest by reducing contention on the zone lock and shortening callback duration.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/3] mm/page_alloc: disable IRQs around the remaining pcp drains
series_items.patch_summary: This patch disables interrupts around the remaining pcp drains in the Linux kernel's page allocation code to prevent potential deadlocks caused by interrupt handlers running while holding the pcp lock. The patch introduces a new macro, `pcp_spin_unlock_nopin_irqrestore`, which saves and restores the interrupt flags when dropping the pcp lock. This change is particularly important for systems with many CPUs, as it reduces the likelihood of deadlock situations. The patch has been tested on a 128-vCPU guest and has shown significant improvements in performance by reducing the frequency of fallbacks to the TLB remove table RCU callbacks.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism by modifying the handling of interrupts and locks. The problem arises when IRQs are disabled to prevent deadlocks, allowing interrupt handlers to fire before tasks can release their locks. This leads to increased contention on the zone lock, causing softlockups. To resolve this, the patch series reorders the locking sequence so that IRQs remain disabled until after the pcp lock is released, giving interrupt handlers a better chance of acquiring the pcp lock and reducing contention on the zone lock.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH bpf-next v3 0/4] bpf: Check recursion per task for preemptible programs
Re: [PATCH bpf-next v3 0/4] bpf: Check recursion per task for preemptible programs
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch proposes a new approach to concurrency-safe private stacks in Linux, which are currently used by BPF programs. The existing per-prog per-cpu model is not sufficient for concurrent tasks on the same CPU, leading to potential corruption and overflow/underflow issues. The proposed solution introduces a per-prog per-cpu pool of private stacks, where each program acquires an available slot at invocation time and releases it on exit. This allows multiple tasks to use separate private stacks concurrently, eliminating the need for marking private stacks and enabling the use of a new per-task per-prog recursion guard. The patch is a proof-of-concept implementation for x86_64 trampolines and has been validated with bpftrace programs.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] x86/efi: Handle EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY in do_add_efi_memmap()
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds handling for EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY in the do_add_efi_memmap() function, which is responsible for adding memory mappings to the kernel. When unaccepted memory is reported by the EFI stub, it was previously ignored and added as reserved memory instead of RAM. This patch changes the behavior so that unaccepted memory is treated as RAM when CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY is enabled, allowing the kernel to use this memory. Without CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY, the memory remains reserved.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Do not signal event 0 to a masked PE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents event 0 from being signaled to a masked Performance Extension (PE) in the ARM SDEI firmware driver. When a PE is masked, it should not receive event 0 signals, which can cause other CPUs to hang. The patch introduces a lock and flag system to ensure that event 0 is only signaled to unmasked PEs. It also updates the cpu_pm notifier to correctly handle masking and unmasking of PEs. This fix addresses issues with CPU hangs and panics caused by event 0 signals being sent to masked PEs.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed YinFengwei's concern that sdei_event_signal() could hang if another CPU holds the lock when it tries to signal a masked PE, explaining that in this scenario the other CPU was stopped and would never drop the lock. The author concluded that there is no need for a trylock because the sender has either counted its signal or never sent one.

Author responded to feedback about the potential for a race condition between loading and storing the unmasked flag, explaining that the notifier runs with IRQs off and only this CPU writes the flag, making it safe.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a lockup issue on idle CPUs caused by SDEI NMI backtraces. The problem occurs when an event is signaled to all CPUs, including those in a power-down state where SDEI is masked. To fix this, the patches prevent event 0 from being sent to masked PEs and send regular backtrace IPIs to these CPUs instead. This approach ensures that the system remains responsive even during idle states.

review_comments.raw_body:
The SDEI NMI backtrace signals event 0 to every other CPU, including the
ones in a power-down idle state, where the kernel has SDEI masked. TF-A

The author explains that no store can race with this load due to the IRQs being off, but acknowledges that other types of interrupts (stop or panic from an SDEI event or pseudo-NMI) could still interrupt it. No fix is planned.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

version_history.subject: [PATCH] drm/i915/gem: Skip writeback of shmem folios with extra references

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the drm/i915/gem module to skip writeback of shmem folios that have extra references, preventing a race condition where a stale TLB entry can still store data to an unmapped folio until the TLB is flushed. The change ensures that such folios are left to reclaim as mapped ones would be, rather than being written back from swap without the stored data.

review_comments.author: Andi Shyti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Andi Shyti noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio has extra references beyond the page cache and writeback_iter(), which can lead to stale TLB entries allowing writes through, and requested checking for this condition in addition to the existing folio_mapped() check.

Reviewer Andi Shyti pointed out that the patch is unnecessary because the i915 writeback iterator already skips shmem folios in the described case, making the new refcount check redundant.

review_comments.summary: Author realized that __shmem_writeback() never runs for shmem folios due to PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY not being set, and questions the purpose of writeback in this context.
review_comments.raw_body:
Oh. It took me a while to see why.

__shmem_writeback() asks writeback_iter() for PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY
folios, and shmem never sets that tag, its ->dirty_folio is
noop_dirty_folio(). So the loop body never runs for any folio, and
hasn't since 776a853a43c9 ("i915: Use writeback_iter()").

That makes me question the whole writeback thing. What's going on
there, and what's the plan?

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.summary: Christoph Hellwig expressed strong disagreement with the patch, stating that it's an indication of a deeper issue in drm code managing tmpfs and suggested removing the problematic code path altogether.
review_comments.raw_body:
I (and others) have been asking forever to get drm out of micro-managing
tmpfs.  I guess given that this code path hasn't worked for a year and
a half is a pretty good indicator that this instance should simply
go away.

review_comments.author: Joonas Lahtinen
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Joonas Lahtinen expressed frustration that patches are being pushed without proper review and maintenance, specifically mentioning the introduction of regressions and lack of Cc'ing maintainers.

Reviewer Joonas Lahtinen expressed strong disagreement with the patch, citing that the writeback for dirty shmem pages was a complex issue that took multiple years to address and is more likely to occur on older hardware. He questioned whether the patch's authors would take responsibility for reverting or fixing the potential issues it may cause.
review_comments.raw_body:
Not so funny to me, you folks are pushing regressions without ever
Cc'ing a single maintainer in the original patches.

I was under impression that Linux development had some rules about
not introducing regressions and also some rules about not pushing
stuff silently to other subsystems. Maybe it's just me not able to
keep up with the vibes of these times.

---

That's not a good indicator in this case.

The writeback for dirty shmem pages took multiple years and multiple
iterations to address the best we could as it's not exactly a race
that shows up frequently.

It's also more likely on the hardware from the era the fix was developed
on, and the owners of those older machines are not exactly jumping to the
latest mainline but rather more likely to run Debian oldstable.

So which one of you will be writing up a revert or fix for the offending
patch or do you expect us to clean up the mess you've created?

Regards, Joonas

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3 0/3] mm: make watermark checks honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3 0/3] mm: make watermark checks honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, which takes into account the migratetype of the request when checking if an allocation can succeed. The function is used in several places where the caller needs to know whether the allocation will honor ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests. The patch also moves the declaration of __zone_watermark_ok() to mm/page_alloc.h and makes no functional changes yet, as it's a preparation for future changes that will make the high-order check respect ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag. When this flag is set, the check should not consider free pages from other migration types when allocating a high-order request. This change aims to prevent fragmentation and improve performance under memory pressure conditions. The patch also updates the compaction logic to take into account the new watermark check and ensures that allocations do not stall in compaction unnecessarily. As a result, the patch is expected to reduce the number of stalls and failures during 64K mTHP faults under swap pressure.

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain suggested renaming zone_watermark_ok_mt to a more descriptive name, such as zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc, to clarify its purpose and distinguish it from the existing zone_watermark_ok function.
review_comments.raw_body:
zone_watermark_ok_mt is a bad name, I am having a hard time figuring out when
to call zone_watermark_ok and when to call zone_watermark_ok_mt. Let us look at
what zone_watermark_ok answers currently, according to the comment above it:

a) "Return true if free base pages are above 'mark'."
b) "For high-order checks it will return true if the order-0 watermark is reached
    and there is at least one free page of a suitable size".

So there are two uses: whether we have enough free pages, then, whether
we have enough free pages *and* we can also allocate.

So let us do something like: we have zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc. It will call
zone_watermark_ok, which will only handle the watermark computation (so this is a
refactor for the code ending at if (!order) line in current zone_watermark_ok).
Then it will also scan the freelists for the correct order, correct migratetype etc.

Then at the callsite we clearly know whether we are just looking for enough free memory,
or whether we are looking for an allocation too.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Dev Jain's concern that the patch's high-order watermark check does not honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT for callers that pass a high order, specifically kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's __compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). The author explained that these callers need to scan the entire free list without filtering by migratetype, which is not provided by the _mt() helpers. They are open to renaming the _mt() function.
review_comments.raw_body:
A count-only zone_watermark_ok() does not work for three callers that
pass a high order: kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's
__compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). They
ask whether the zone has a free page of that order regardless of
migratetype. They need the free list scan without the migratetype
filter, so neither of your two helpers fits them.

So the split is not count vs scan. It is the zone as a whole vs one
request, as the comment above __zone_watermark_ok() says. The _mt variant
is the one that takes the request's migratetype. Callers that only want
the count already pass order 0.

I am not particularly tied to the _mt() name, but _for_alloc() is a
mouthful.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Dev Jain clarified that they wanted to enforce the same rules as below the if (!order) check in __zone_watermark_ok() for ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests, regarding migratetypes and orders while scanning freelists.

Reviewer Dev Jain expressed concern that the patch introduces inconsistency by using both alloc_flags and migratetype to determine the allocation context, which can lead to confusion in existing callers.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think my wording was unclear. By "correct migratetype etc." I did not mean
"only the requested migratetype". I meant the same rules being enforced
below the if (!order) check in current __zone_watermark_ok(), in relation
to the migratetypes and orders while scanning the freelists.

---

Although I thought a lot last week and my approach would cause more churn due
to changing lots of places to _for_alloc, so I am fine with your approach for
now. But read on.

Currently you pass migratetype and you say in the comment in patch 1:

"Use __zone_watermark_ok_mt() instead to check whether a particular allocation
can be served."

But, for the existing callers who pass order > 0 , aren't they also checking
whether the allocation can be served? It is confusing me that both alloc_flags
and migratetype are logically part of the "allocation context" but some
callers are doing alloc_flags & ~ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT ... I am not sure whether
the below Sashiko report is related to that, I didn't check in detail:

https://sashiko.dev/#/patchset/20261116125103.2894162-1-kas%40kernel.org

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author addressed Dev Jain's concern that kswapd and kcompactd should not consider other migratetypes' free lists when determining whether to wake up or compact, explaining that these functions do not have an allocation to serve and thus do not need to consider migratetypes.

Author acknowledged that should_reclaim_retry() is responsible for clearing a flag, not the high-order watermark check, and explained that filtering by migratetype would introduce a new behavior change.
review_comments.raw_body:
No. kswapd's pgdat_balanced() and kcompactd's __compact_finished() have
no allocation to serve. They are woken with an order and balance the
zone for it. There is no migratetype to pass.

should_reclaim_retry() has an allocation, but it asks whether it could
succeed once everything reclaimable is freed, not whether it can be
served now. Its order-0 part already counts reclaimable pages as free.

---

Only should_reclaim_retry() clears it, and that is what Sashiko flagged.
It keeps what the check did there before the series: it never filtered
by migratetype.

Filtering would send movable order-2/3 requests, like 16K/32K mTHP
faults in a MADV_HUGEPAGE region, to compaction retries and the fallback
sooner. That is a behaviour change of its own and needs its own numbers.
Out-of-scope for the patchset.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass the allocation's flags down to try_to_free_pages(). Specifically, it records ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT in scan_control and uses this information to determine whether a costly order can succeed. This change is intended to improve performance by allowing direct reclaim to take advantage of free pages that are not movable or reclaimable. The patch was tested on Dev Jain's 64K mTHP benchmark and showed improved results, freeing more pages during direct reclaim with defrag_mode enabled.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue caused by the high-order watermark check not honouring the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag in memory pressure situations. The check currently counts free pages of every migratetype, leading to incorrect results and stalls in compaction. The patches modify the watermark checks to take into account the request's migratetype and skip free lists that cannot be used. This is achieved by passing the alloc_flags to try_to_free_pages() and modifying the should_reclaim_retry() function. The changes are based on a benchmark that shows significant improvements in performance, with 64K mTHP faults under memory pressure stalling 18 times less often than without the patch series.

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain suggested renaming zone_watermark_ok to handle two distinct use cases: checking if there are enough free pages and checking if there are enough free pages that can be allocated, by introducing a new function zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc.
review_comments.raw_body:
zone_watermark_ok_mt is a bad name, I am having a hard time figuring out when
to call zone_watermark_ok and when to call zone_watermark_ok_mt. Let us look at
what zone_watermark_ok answers currently, according to the comment above it:

a) "Return true if free base pages are above 'mark'."
b) "For high-order checks it will return true if the order-0 watermark is reached
    and there is at least one free page of a suitable size".

So there are two uses: whether we have enough free pages, then, whether
we have enough free pages *and* we can also allocate.

So let us do something like: we have zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc. It will call
zone_watermark_ok, which will only handle the watermark computation (so this is a
refactor for the code ending at if (!order) line in current zone_watermark_ok).
Then it will also scan the freelists for the correct order, correct migratetype etc.

Then at the callsite we clearly know whether we are just looking for enough free memory,
or whether we are looking for an allocation too.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Dev's concern that the zone_watermark_ok() function does not work for callers that pass a high order, explaining that it is not about count vs scan but rather about the zone as a whole vs one request. The author acknowledged that these callers need the free list scan without the migratetype filter and suggested renaming the _mt variant to something more descriptive.
review_comments.raw_body:
A count-only zone_watermark_ok() does not work for three callers that
pass a high order: kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's
__compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). They
ask whether the zone has a free page of that order regardless of
migratetype. They need the free list scan without the migratetype
filter, so neither of your two helpers fits them.

So the split is not count vs scan. It is the zone as a whole vs one
request, as the comment above __zone_watermark_ok() says. The _mt variant
is the one that takes the request's migratetype. Callers that only want
the count already pass order 0.

I am not particularly tied to the _mt() name, but _for_alloc() is a
mouthful.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not correctly enforce the requested migratetype when scanning freelists, specifically below the if (!order) check in __zone_watermark_ok(), and requested clarification on how the rules are being enforced

Reviewer Dev Jain noted that the patch's approach to passing migratetype and alloc_flags is inconsistent, as some callers check allocation context using alloc_flags & ~ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT while others use __zone_watermark_ok_mt(), causing confusion.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think my wording was unclear. By "correct migratetype etc." I did not mean
"only the requested migratetype". I meant the same rules being enforced
below the if (!order) check in current __zone_watermark_ok(), in relation
to the migratetypes and orders while scanning the freelists.

---

Although I thought a lot last week and my approach would cause more churn due
to changing lots of places to _for_alloc, so I am fine with your approach for
now. But read on.

Currently you pass migratetype and you say in the comment in patch 1:

"Use __zone_watermark_ok_mt() instead to check whether a particular allocation
can be served."

But, for the existing callers who pass order > 0 , aren't they also checking
whether the allocation can be served? It is confusing me that both alloc_flags
and migratetype are logically part of the "allocation context" but some
callers are doing alloc_flags & ~ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT ... I am not sure whether
the below Sashiko report is related to that, I didn't check in detail:

https://sashiko.dev/#/patchset/20261116125103.2894162-1-kas%40kernel.org

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed Dev Jain's concern that the watermark check in kswapd's pgdat_balanced() and kcompactd's __compact_finished() should pass a migratetype, explaining that these functions do not have an allocation to serve and therefore do not need to consider migratypes. The author also clarified that should_reclaim_retry() already counts reclaimable pages as free for order-0 allocations.

Author addressed a concern about should_reclaim_retry() clearing the per-vswap spinlock, explaining that it's only cleared by this function and that filtering by migratetype would introduce a new behavior change requiring its own numbers.
review_comments.raw_body:
No. kswapd's pgdat_balanced() and kcompactd's __compact_finished() have
no allocation to serve. They are woken with an order and balance the
zone for it. There is no migratetype to pass.

should_reclaim_retry() has an allocation, but it asks whether it could
succeed once everything reclaimable is freed, not whether it can be
served now. Its order-0 part already counts reclaimable pages as free.

---

Only should_reclaim_retry() clears it, and that is what Sashiko flagged.
It keeps what the check did there before the series: it never filtered
by migratetype.

Filtering would send movable order-2/3 requests, like 16K/32K mTHP
faults in a MADV_HUGEPAGE region, to compaction retries and the fallback
sooner. That is a behaviour change of its own and needs its own numbers.
Out-of-scope for the patchset.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH 1/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Do not signal event 0 to a masked PE
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch modifies the firmware: arm_sdei module to prevent event 0 from being signaled to a masked Processing Element (PE). The change ensures that the lock is not held indefinitely, which could lead to a panic hanging on it. Instead, the code checks if the PE is unmasked and only signals the event if it is.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author is addressing concerns about potential deadlocks in the smp_send_stop() path when signaling events to masked PEs. They explained that since the notifier runs with IRQs off, no store can race with the load of the flag from another CPU, and KCSAN will report any changes.

The author is addressing a concern about potential data races in the notifier's access to pe->unmasked, specifically whether it needs to use READ_ONCE() and WRITE_ONCE(). The author explains that since the notifier runs with IRQs off, no store can race with this load. They also mention that KCSAN will report any changes to this behavior.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that sdei_block_signal() can be called during a panic, which occurs in the smp_send_stop() path, and this could lead to a deadlock if another CPU is stopped in the middle of signalling an event

Ah. Yes. This is the key point. If it's panic and trying to do
